The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B , with Cursor crossing $4.6B ), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025 , and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models ( balesni ). Goodfire acquisition talks : The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs ( report ). Other integrity signals : Benchmark contamination : Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval ( Karvonen ). Incident taxonomy : OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents ( framework ). Disclosure policy : Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities ( policy ). items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.content: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.content: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. Show notes BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. FLUX 3 launch and research overview Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. FLUX 3 Video demos See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. FLUX Kontext examples Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. Guest bio · Original research Dustin Podell led FLUX Kontext and was the lead author of SDXL. Dustin’s project credits · FLUX Kontext · SDXL The first Latent Space essay grew out of the Stable Diffusion release. items.title: datasette 1.0a43
items.content: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) Open-source AI without Jensen
items.content: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out. Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models. There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety” . Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting. Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work. As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king. The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen. Share The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis emergency podcast : Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it. Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot

items.content: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

Specs and pricing : The model offers four thinking levels (low, medium, high and xhigh) and a 1M context window. Google says this reaches near-Carbon success on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 24% less quota and 19% faster completion. It is rolling out to Ultra subscribers ( Google , Mohan ). Strengths : Hydrogen has an 8% hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience, versus 43% for Sonnet and 52% for Sol. It also shares the #1 score on GDP.pdf visual reasoning. Weaknesses : It scores 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at both high and xhigh, below Sonnet at 64% and Sol at 56%. Third-party leaderboards : Agent Arena : Hydrogen debuts at #5 with +14.8% net improvement across 6.5k sessions. It is the fastest model in the top 10 at 5.3 minutes per task median, with a median cost of $1.6 per task ( Arena ). Code Arena WebDev : It ranks #10 with 1703 points ( Arena ). Vals Index : It is #6 at 68.5%, 2 points behind Carbon at 38% of Carbon's price ( Vals ). Coding agents : CursorBench rises to 54.3% from 39.6% for 3.8 Flash ( Cursor ). Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 shows 38.2%, just behind Sol ( Cognition ). SWE-sweep shows 13.5%, versus 9.5% for Astra ( KLieret ). Caveats from users : Runaway reasoning : One tester saw xhigh spend 131K thinking tokens and about $1.08 without answering a jersey-number image question. The same tester reports budget exhaustion on 1.8% of a text benchmark ( skalskip92 ). Weak spots : Hydrogen scored 1% on MazeBench ( patience_cave ). Pricing structure : Simon Willison says Hydrogen is only a 25% discount on the Carbon/Argon token price, though those models reportedly double in price on Dec 1 ( simonw ). Speed : Theo disputes the "built for speed" framing based on his own timings ( theo ). Architecture : New components include attention residuals with a q/k/v split, gated attention, a dynamic attention sink, dynamic shortconv and value norm ( Songlin Yang ). Experts use NVFP4 in layers 0–39 and MXFP8 in the last eight, with SWA widened to 1k and softcaps on the LM head and SwiGLU ( eliebakouch ). Day-0 serving : On vLLM, it fits on one GB200/GB300 node and reaches up to 630 tok/s per user at TP4. Its native DSpark speculator has an acceptance length of about 3.5 at T=1.0 ( vLLM , details ). Evals : It is the #1 US open model on Code Arena WebDev at 1647 points ( Arena ). On Agent Arena it is #2 among open models, with a median cost of $0.26 per task ( Arena ). It also holds the top open-model spot on MathArena's BrokenArXiv ( MathArena ). Edge0-145B/120B : These are device-native open-weight models. items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.content: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0 , when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible . Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. ( The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe , their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic. ” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers . “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. It struck a nerve with people. They felt sort of maligned by Adobe and other tech companies . And what we built has really resonated with them.” After his presentation, Thomas was mobbed by AIE Code attendees. ArtCraft’s apps are being downloaded at the rate of about 1.7 million per day, which Thomas said is still accelerating. In addition to the 17 official apps, there are around 300 being developed by the community, he added. Rust is key, but there have been technical challenges Other than the AI technology, Thomas said that Rust was a crucial part of making the apps performant — he claimed that PhotoCraft opens ten times faster than Photoshop, for example. “Rust was probably essential in this product's success,” he said. “We've seen people do it in Electron before, but for high-quality creative apps, you really need something that's native. ” For those engineers who are not experts in Rust, Thomas has good news for you. “Do you need to know Rust to start using Rust today as an engineer? items.content: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search. Tags: gemini , llm , google , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-pricing , ai , llms

items.title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
items.content: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate. ” How Glean uses Jev With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Jev patterns and prototypes Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath , a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks . They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second , even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust ,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts , a Principal Engineer at Workday , finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” Like the early internet The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software . I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an explosion of what software can do, and we will want people to be exploring those boundaries of software. Not necessarily because it's valuable, but because they can, because we have new frontiers to explore , and this is what the early internet was like.”

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.content: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.content: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.content: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloud Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Dots Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user. The first is as a safety net — your dot can flag things you may have missed. The second is as “a delegation sink” ; Guo said he uses it “a ton in Slack” for this reason. And the third is as a ubiquitous presence . “I think the third way that dots are a little bit different is we're aiming to make them truly everywhere that you work ,” Guo said. items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.content: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notes Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.content: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter . Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding . As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis . Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: Model Intelligence Index DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 GLM-5.3-Flash: 43 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench . The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card , Naive AI – Research . Model NL2Repo-Bench DeepSWE v1.1 Agent's Last Exam (ALE) GLM-5.3-Flash 56.3 63.4 26.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 68.2 77.0 35.4 Naive-N0.5-Flash 71.9 67.8 32.4 Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed and verbosity experiments Speed is the headline feature. 1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly. 2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500 , 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond . That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity . The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind. Graphic by Gabriele Beltramo Key observations Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput , approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash. Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average. The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models. The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) , at 89.8 seconds against 79.7. Two caveats apply.
